This substantial body size is accompanied by an ultimate wet weight for female individuals of approximately 7200 grams [Wwi = approximately 7200 grams], a value that positions Varanus bengalensis among the larger-bodied members of its genus in the Indian subcontinent. The attainment of this asymptotic mass requires several years of sustained feeding, during which the juvenile and sub-adult must navigate the risks of predation, resource competition, and intermittent food availability.

The deposition of eggs occurs in excavated burrows or termite mounds, where incubation proceeds for the duration determined by local thermal conditions. Post-oviposition, females provide no parental care, and the emerging yolk-sac larvae are entirely independent from the moment of shell pipping. The energetic commitment to reproduction is therefore front-loaded, concentrated entirely into egg formation and laying. The energetic costs of tissue upkeep, or basal maintenance requirements, scale with body mass and account for a substantial fraction of the daily ingested energy in these large adults. Comparative analyses within the Varanidae suggest that body size and longevity are positively correlated across clades, with the Bengal monitor occupying an intermediate position between the smaller, shorter-lived arid-zone goannas and the truly giant species such as the Komodo dragon.

Maximum documented longevity in the Bengal monitor, based on captive records and mark-recapture data from wild populations, extends to approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is characteristic of a relatively slow-paced life history strategy, wherein the costs of achieving a large adult body size are offset by an extended reproductive window spanning multiple decades. Physiological death in this species typically results from the progressive deterioration of organ function associated with senescence, rather than from acute starvation or disease. The capacity to store substantial lipid reserves during periods of prey abundance provides a buffer against seasonal fluctuations in resource availability, contributing to the species' resilience across its broad geographic range. The long-lived nature of the Bengal monitor, coupled with its moderate fecundity, underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparous reproduction over a single, high-risk reproductive event.
